thread.title: Apple: Key IPhone Suppliers Don't Seem To Be Cutting Back - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Mark Hibben
title: Apple: Key IPhone Suppliers Don't Seem To Be Cutting Back - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Rethink Technology business briefs for December 21, 2018.
Monthly revenue reports from Foxconn, Pegatron and TSMC don't support the iPhone cutback narrative
iPhone XS Logic Board with three mystery audio amplifiers. Source: iFixit.
Much has been written recently about supposed production cuts to Apple's ( AAPL ) iPhone in the December quarter and beyond. Many analysts now reasonably assume that iPhone unit sales will decline in the December quarter, and noted Apple analyst Ming-Chi Kuo already has cut his forecast for calendar 2019 Q1, based on what he assessed as lower than expected demand for iPhone XR.
Largely ignored by this narrative is what's going on at three key Taiwanese suppliers, Hon Hai Precision Industries (known as Foxconn), Pegatron and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company ( TSM ). These companies report revenues on a monthly basis, and so can give investors and analysts insight into what's happening with iPhone production before Apple reports its December quarter results.
Hon Hai is the main iPhone assembler, and Pegatron is thought to be the primary assembler of the lower-cost iPhone XR. TSMC is the world's largest semiconductor foundry and has been the sole source of the iPhone's main processor since the iPhone 7. Thus TSMC supplies the processors for all the iPhones that Apple currently sells.
The monthly revenue reports are available on the websites of Hon Hai , Pegatron and TSMC . Pegatron and TSMC have reported their results through November, while Hon Hai has only posted through October. However, Bloomberg has reported Hon Hai's revenue for November, so I'm using Bloomberg's revenue number. The table below summarizes the results for these companies.
All three companies posted strong y/y revenue gains for the first two months of the December quarter. Of the three, only TSMC has provided guidance for Q4, and I've provided a year-over-year percent change in revenue for the second half of 2018 based on their guidance. TSMC provided very conservative guidance for its Q4, and its monthly revenues seem to be running well ahead of guidance.
The surge at Pegatron in November seems to correlate with a report that Pegatron is the main iPhone XR assembler, with the late release of iPhone XR in October. Pegatron's relatively weak Q3 may indicate that Apple was “saving” Pegatron for XR production while dedicating Hon Hai to the top end XS and XS Max models.
Of course, there's no guarantee that things won't go to hell in December, but I would have thought that production cuts would have started to show up in November if iPhone sales were really as bad as many think. And all three companies do business outside of Apple, so that kind of muddies the waters as well. But generally, for the December quarter, the assemblers get most of their revenue from Apple.
Part of the problem with the cutback reports is that they never specify from what level of production the cut occurred. Even if there are further cuts in December, they would be coming off fairly high production levels in October and November. The net result for the quarter might still be a year over year gain. Fortunately, investors will probably be afforded the opportunity to see the revenue numbers for December before Apple reports.
A closer look at the revised guidance issued by some Apple suppliers Four key Apple suppliers, Cirrus Logic ( CRUS ), AMS AG ( OTCPK:AMSSY ), Lumentum ( LITE ) and Qorvo ( QRVO ), all issued revised guidance for calendar Q4 which seemed to imply that massive cutbacks to iPhone production were underway for the December quarter. Once again, the problem is knowing the prior level of production.
The production ramp for the new iPhone generation actually begins in calendar Q3, and for second tier suppliers such as the group mentioned above, may even begin before Q3. As I show in the table below, all of them except Cirrus showed robust y/y growth in Q3.
Based on the growth the suppliers enjoyed in Q3, it appears that Apple wanted to get an early start to the iPhone production ramp and make sure that it had plenty of inventory for the launch. Yet Apple reported flat unit sales of iPhone for the September quarter (0.45% year-over-year growth), suggesting that the supply chain over produced in the quarter. Any excess inventory would naturally be carried over into calendar Q4.
The need to make the correction in inventory is probably what drove Apple to rein in its suppliers in November. By that time, iPhone XR had been released, and Apple probably had a pretty good feel for what it would need by way of production to finish out the quarter. Does that mean that quarterly unit sales of iPhone would fall below last year?
Not necessarily. The best way to gauge how Apple will do is to look at the calendar Q3 results combined with the Q4 guidance. This is calculated as an H2 y/y % change, which is positive for all the companies except Cirrus. Were it not for Cirrus, this would indicate that Apple's December quarter will probably have positive unit growth year-over-year.
What of Cirrus? Cirrus has become the poster child of the supposed iPhone downturn, but it may not be a good indicator. Although Cirrus is thought to generate about 80% of its revenue from Apple, Cirrus was hit by a Cirrus-unique cutback when Apple decided to omit the lightning-to-headphone dongle from all iPhones in its current line-up, going back as far as the iPhone 7. Cirrus provided the D/A converter chip and audio amplifier contained in the dongle.
In addition to dongle loss, Cirrus may have lost some content on the new iPhones. In the most recent teardowns of the iPhone XS and XS Max conducted by iFixit and TechInsights , audio amplifiers normally attributed to Cirrus were instead labeled as Apple chips by both companies. Apple may have taken over design and manufacturing of the chips and given Cirrus a royalty fee only for whatever Cirrus IP Apple might be using. This also would reduce Cirrus revenue per device.
This is somewhat speculative, of course, but Apple is known to already have done something similar with Dialog Semiconductor's ( OTCPK:DLGNF ) power management ICs. In October Apple spent $600 million to purchase assets, IP and transfer employees from Dialog in order to bring the power management chip design under Apple's control.
Or it could be that Apple is simply using a different supplier for the audio amplifiers. There are certainly numerous suppliers available. So Cirrus seems to be an outlier that's not really representative of the overall trend of H2 y/y growth for Apple's component suppliers.
Lumentum may represent the best pathway to scaling production changes in iPhone. Lumentum supplies the lasers used in Apple's exclusive TrueDepth 3D sensor for FaceID security on iPhone X, XS, XR, XS Max and the new iPad Pros. Lumentum does not currently supply production quantities of the device to any other smartphone maker.
Lumentum reports sales of its 3D sensor lasers in a separate category (Industrial and Consumer) that we can assume is virtually all Apple. It was Lumentum that initiated the production cut back worries when it issued revised guidance on November 12:
"We recently received a request from one of our largest Industrial and Consumer customers for laser diodes for 3D sensing to materially reduce shipments to them during our fiscal second quarter for previously placed orders that were originally scheduled for delivery during the quarter," said Alan Lowe, President and CEO.
It was clear that all of the reduction in revenue guidance, $72.5 million, was due to scaling back 3D sensing laser production. From this we can get a pretty good idea of where total 3D sensing laser production wound up for calendar H2, as shown in the table below:
The numbers for Industrial and Consumer revenue are as reported except for the initial and revised guidance for Q4, where I had to make an educated guess, since Lumentum doesn't provide that granular guidance. My guess for the initial Q4 guidance is based on comparing with last year's (calendar 2017 Q4) results. For the revised guidance, I subtracted the full $72.5 million delta the Industrial and Consumer revenue.
Then, I compare the revised guidance estimate for H2 revenue with last year. Overall, H2 doesn't look that bad, and even the Industrial and Consumer revenue shows 4.74% year-over-year growth.
Investor takeaways I'd be the first to admit that nothing I've presented in this article constitutes conclusive proof that Apple will grow unit sales of iPhone in the December quarter. Indeed Apple's guidance of tepid 3% year-over-year revenue growth in calendar Q4 implies some iPhone unit decline. However, the picture that emerges from Apple's suppliers is not of a dramatic decline. In fact, there's some reason to believe that Apple will beat guidance and achieve single-digit unit growth for the iPhone.
Right now, the market seems to be terrified of a big iPhone unit sales decline, and I just don't think that's in the cards at all. At this point, I'm cautiously optimistic that Apple will beat guidance, but I'm just not sure by how much.
And I wanted to illustrate the process I go through in arriving at my estimates for Apple earnings that I publish in advance for Rethink Technology subscribers. Rarely are analysts afforded “conclusive proof” of anything pertaining to their earnings forecasts. Most of the evidence is “circumstantial” but nevertheless has in the past afforded me a pathway to fairly accurate earnings predictions. I'll be keeping a close eye on December revenue reports and other data in order to generate my final earnings estimates.
In the long run, I view Apple as a terrific investment regardless of any individual quarter's results especially at current valuation. I remain long Apple and rate it a buy.
